0.text: Most buyers pay three times more premium on 1 oz coins than on 10 oz bars.
On 100 oz, that difference is $416 in real money.

1.text: When you buy a 1 oz Silver Eagle, you pay 12 to 22 percent above the spot price of silver.
That covers minting, distribution, and dealer margin.
At $32 per ounce spot, the total cost runs between $35.

2.text: A 10 oz silver bar from a major bullion mint costs 4 to 6 percent over spot.
At $32 per ounce spot, that puts your total cost between $33.
That is a meaningful difference from coins.

3.text: Buying 100 Silver Eagles at 18 percent premium costs $3,776.
Buying 10 x 10 oz bars at 5 percent costs $3,360.
That buys more than 12 additional ounces of silver at spot.

4.text: The chart shows premium ranges by product type.
Generic bars cost around 5 percent over spot.
Government-minted Silver Eagles carry the highest premium at around 18 percent.
The format you choose determines how much silver you actually get for your dollar.

5.text: Storage is where the format really shows its cost.
One hundred individual coins need 100 capsules, five storage tubes, or a chunk of a monster box.
Ten bars stack flat and take up a fraction of the space.
For a home safe, bars are the smarter fit.

6.text: American Silver Eagles are the most recognized silver product in the USA.
Dealers pay $1 to $3 above their buy price per ounce on Eagles.
Generic 10 oz bars usually sell at or near spot on the resale side.

7.text: Below 50 ounces, the dollar difference between coins and bars is real but modest.
Most buyers building a serious position choose bars for the bulk of their stack and add coins selectively.

8.text: Choose bars for maximum silver per dollar, long-term holds, and home safe storage.
Choose coins when you want to sell individual pieces, prefer the most liquid silver format
or plan to give silver as a gift.
Most buyers end up holding both.
